title: LLM inference papers + conference harvest (Jan–Mar 2026)
content:
Purpose: quick personal harvest from papers + a couple conference talks I attended. Focus is practical tips we can test in Redwood Dedicated/Private: batching, KV/cache, quantization tradeoffs, and measuring realistic SLOs. Mostly bullety notes and follow-ups for next 6 weeks.

High-level takeaways (one-liners)
- Don’t trust synthetic perf curves: tail latency and cold-KV behavior change ranking of optimizations. Need prefix-heavy traces.
- 4-bit quantization methods make sense for ~70–90% of customer traffic, but certain instruction patterns (rotary, special attention kernels) cause quality cliffs. Must gate by model+prompt family.
- Continuous batching + adaptive batch sizing (based on latency budget) is low-hanging fruit for throughput without regressing p50 by much.
- Caching prefixes + proactive prefetch for expected next-token requests helped 15–30% token-cost reductions in the paper’s web-scale trace. Worth reproducing on our logs.

Papers / talks worth reading (short notes)
1) "Dynamic KV Prefetching for Low-Latency Inference" (arXiv 2026-01) – link above
   - Idea: predict which key-value cache shards will be needed within next 50ms and warm them on idle cycles.
   - Empirical: 18% p95 improvement for conversational apps with short turns.
   - My notes: prediction model is tiny (decision tree on token entropy + turn length). Cheap to run on CPU.
   - Follow-up: try classifier on our conversation logs (CS-provided sample) and measure prefetch hit rate.

2) "Robust 4-bit Quant for Transformer MLPs" (NeurIPS 2026 talk)
   - Hybrid quant (per-channel for first and last FFN matmuls, group-wise for middle) preserves accuracy.
   - Latency win depends on kernel coverage (our runtime needs more fused 4-bit GEMM kernels).
   - Action: inventory models used in Hosted API vs Dedicated to see which have compatible architecture for hybrid quant.

3) "Workload-driven batching: adaptive latency-aware schedulers" (ICLR workshop)
   - Scheduler uses per-request latency budget, current queue length, and estimated service time to pick batch size.
   - Simulation in paper shows 25% throughput vs static batching under bursty arrivals.
   - Relevance: we have telemetry to compute per-request budgets (route-level SLO). Could prototype as a dev feature flag.

Conference tidbits (from Feb workshop sessions)
- Talk: "Measuring user-perceived latency in chat apps" – folks instrumented client-side perceived latency not just server token generation. Interesting correlation with prefix-cache misses.
- Panel: "When to fall back to smaller models" – consensus: degrade gracefully (partial output + compressed reason) rather than abrupt switch. Also prefer model-variant ensembles for hallucination-sensitive routes.
- Poster: inference cost attribution by token type (system vs user vs assistant) — helpful for per-route pricing experiments.

Small experiments I ran locally (scratch)
- Microbench: continuous batching heuristic (increase batch size while p50 < target) on a trimmed Llama-like model. Result: throughput +40% on sustained QPS but p99 spikes during cold-starts.
- Quant test: naive 4-bit quant with per-tensor scale caused visible rouge scores drop on summarization dataset. Hybrid per-channel fixes most drop.
- Prefetch sim: offline sim on 72k convo traces -> prefetch classifier hit rate ~0.62, warms reduce p95 by ~12% in simulation. Realization: our storage layer can’t saturate small prefetch loads; there’s an engineering cost.

Open questions / unknowns
- How well does prefetching play with multi-tenant Dedicated where KV stores are shared? Risk: noisy neighbors evict warmed shards. Need eviction policy experiments.
- What percentage of hosted traffic falls into the "safe for 4-bit" bucket by model/route? We should compute this using eval prompts + automatic metrics.
- Does our runtime scheduler have enough telemetry to implement latency-aware batching? Implementability risk: estimating per-request service time accurately for many different model variants.

Concrete follow-ups (owner: Alex unless noted)
1) Data task: generate a stratified sample of route+prompt families (2k prompts) and run cheap quality checks comparing float32 vs our candidate 4-bit config. Output: coverage matrix by route (owner: Maya). Target 2 weeks.
2) Bench task: prototype adaptive-batching scheduler in dev branch with a feature flag. Measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput on standard replay traces. (owner: me + infra). Target 3 weeks.
3) Prefetch POC: run classifier on 10k convo traces and simulate warmed-KV on ded-dev infra; report resource overhead (owner: Samir). Target 4 weeks.
4) Infra checklist: inventory kernels that would block 4-bit perf wins; file infra tickets for missing fused kernels and quantized attention (owner: infra).

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep an eye on any arXiv updates to the dynamic-KV paper — authors plan to open-source their small predictor.
- When running evals, compare both ROUGE/EM and subjective spot checks for instruction-following prompts (some quality regressions are subtle).
- Talk to pricing about whether token-level attribution by token-type is interesting for upcoming Dedicated pilots.

Random scribbles / fragments
- Could we do a per-customer "safe-quant profile"? store profile -> route automatically uses profile if customer config allows.
- Edge case: long-context docs where per-token context distribution differs heavily (code vs email). Might need route-specific quant tuning.

References (quick links I saved)
- Dynamic KV prefetch paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01234
- Proto-bench issue where we tried adaptive batching last year: https://github.com/redwood-inference/proto-bench/issues/412
- Related Confluence: CONFLUENCE-9876 (prefetch design notes)

If I don’t revisit: ping me in 2 weeks to sync with Maya on dataset sampling.

End of note.
